utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen, the technical booth, the interpreters. I see they are there. Good morning to the court reporters, legal assistants. Good morning, Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Harmon, Mr. Krstic, Mr. Visnjic, Mr. Petrusic. Good morning, Professor Brunborg. I hope I pronounce your name correctly. How are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will pronounce it better than I can, I'm sure. You're going to read the solemn declaration that the usher is going to give you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Thank you very much for coming. I think you are very familiar with the court proceedings, so you will be feeling at ease in the courtroom. First of all, you will be answering questions put to you by Mr. McCloskey. Mr. McCloskey, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you please state your name and spell your last name for the record?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: My name is Helge Brunborg. My last name is spelled B-r-u-n-b-o-r-g.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you're of Norwegian nationality?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I'm a demographer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for us what demography is, as relates to your profession?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Demography relates to population studies, the changes of population, and the composition of a population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us your educational background?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. I have an undergraduate degree from the University of Oslo in mathematics and statistics and physics, and a graduate degree from the University of Oslo in economics, and a PhD from the University of Michigan in economics, specialising in demography.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us your employment history?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I've been employed at Statistics Norway since 1974, but with several spells of employment elsewhere, mostly in other countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What is Statistics Norway?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It's a central agency for collecting and disseminating statistics for Norway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you give us an example or two of the kind of work you've done for Statistics Norway over the years?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I made population projections for Norway, for the country and for all the regions. I've studied fertility trends, historically and current, even new patterns, cohabitational patterns, consensual unions, that is, living together without being married, mortality trends in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You say you've had various periods of leave. Can you tell us some of the projects you were involved in during those periods of leave?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I've been employed by the Central Statistics Office of Botswana and by the University of Botswana for two years altogether. I have worked here for one and a half years on a permanent basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Tell us what you were doing in Botswana.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I was working in the demography unit and advising on analysis of census. And I was planning a demographic survey, an interview survey, and in that respect I went into the field with interviewers to collect data.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I notice your curriculum vitae, which is marked Exhibit 269. Under "Professional Activities", can you give us an example of one of your professional activities?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I've been travelling to several countries, advising on various aspects of data collection and data analysis, including Mozambique, Namibia, Zambia, Albania and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you part of the Norwegian delegation to the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. I have represented Norway in the Population Commission of the United Nations since 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was that in regard?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is an advisory body under ECOSOC.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do they do?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: They advise on the population policies and data collection activities and give advice. They were the planning body for the large international population conference in Cairo in 1994, where I was also representing Norway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did you come to work -- to assist the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: End of June, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And while you were working for the Prosecutor, did you get a specific assignment regarding the Srebrenica investigation?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. First I worked on the general problem of estimating the population consequences of the war in Bosnia, and later I was asked to study Srebrenica in particular and try to estimate and validate the number of missing persons from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you basically asked to review the International Committee for the Red Cross's missing list, as well as another missing list from another non-governmental organisation, as well as other material, and determine their potential reliability and validity?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, first of all, can you describe who you worked with on that project and how that was set up?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, first I had an assistant. I've had an assistant since January 1998, because I soon realised that the task, what I was supposed to do, was overwhelming. And these assistants -- there have been four of them -- have been Norwegian graduate students.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have they been they students of yours?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: More or less. Some have, some have -- I've gotten to know through other people, through colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about your teaching experience. What sort of teaching experience do you have?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. I also do part-time teaching at the University of Oslo, and I've been a teacher at the University of Botswana as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what was the team that comprised your population -- your study of Srebrenica missing?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, it was a student, the assistant, and myself, and then we were working in close contact with the team investigating Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is your student's name?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Henrik Urdal and later Torkild Lyngstad, who is here now. I should also mention perhaps that I went back to Oslo in January 1998, 1999, and then worked here on a part-time basis, coming here every two months for a week but then talking to my assistant every day, and he was also coming to Oslo every two months or so, so we had very good contact with the project.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us a bit about how you attacked this project, this task? What was the one of the first things that you had to do?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, first, we needed to find out how the data were collected by these two organisations that you referred to, the ICRC, the International Committee of the Red Cross, and PHR, the Physicians for Human Rights. Is there a problem? Press this one also?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That should get it.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: All right. Now are there two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell the Court what you learned about the ICRC and specifically about their missing lists?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, what I learned was that -- I'm a bit uncomfortable hearing myself in stereo. Can I take this off now? Is that okay? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You'll notice if someone's speaking to you in language you don't understand. Then put it right back on.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. For the time being, if I may. The ICRC is an organisation based in Geneva that has worked for more than a hundred years in relation to war and crisis. It has always emphasised, as far as I know, to be neutral so that they have access to both parties. For instance, visiting prisoners of war. One of their mandates, one of their tasks is to trace people who have gone missing because of the war. In war periods, families easily get split, and if they are refugees or displaced, it's very hard for them to unite. So to help in that, they take tracing requests. People can register people as missing, and they go through various national and international channels to try to locate the missing people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did you learn what specific methods and procedures the ICRC used in regard to the war in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. They had offices all over the former Yugoslavia or particularly in Bosnia and Croatia, and they designed a questionnaire that people who wanted to place a tracing request had to complete with the help of an interviewer and then this information was entered into a database. Parts of the information, some of the items, were published in books.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you, did they allow anyone to come register someone missing or did they have some standards regarding that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Only -- no. Only close relatives were supposed to register, and they had to record the name. In fact, more than 95 per cent of the people who reported a person as missing were close relatives. That is, parents, children, spouses, and siblings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did they ever make exceptions to that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Occasionally friends and neighbours and more distant relatives, because there is a problem in that sometimes whole families went missing and there was nobody to report them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did they allow government agencies or bodies like that to put in missing persons' names?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, and it is not listed, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this was for the entire conflict of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. The first person went listed as missing in Bosnia in November 1991, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many different editions of missing lists has the ICRC actually come out with?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask counsel to make breaks between the questions and answers, please.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Did you say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We speak the same language. We spoke briefly beforehand. I need to make a break and perhaps you can try to make a pause too.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. I'm familiar with the last two editions of this one, this book here, editions 3 and 4. Edition 3 was published in January 1997 and the 4th in July 1998, actually, the 2nd in September 1996, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For the record, that was the Exhibit number 270, the ICRC missing list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So which volumes did you pay attention to in your review?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Volumes 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why wouldn't you just focus on the most recent volume?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Because people were -- between each edition, people were added because more were registered missing, but also people were taken off the list because it was shown that they were dead or, in a few cases, that they were alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that was all of interest to you in forming your final list.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us a little bit about what you learned specifically about the effort to register those missing from Srebrenica by the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I've been told that the whole process started in July 1995, when they learned about the events in Srebrenica. In particular, it started because it became known that many people were captured and were imprisoned in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Those were the allegations or the --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. And it started in Tuzla, where -- because many refugees came to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What have you learned about any problems related to that process?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, it was a very chaotic situation. It must have been when people were separated, especially women and children were separated from the men. They had to flee at very short notice, bringing few belongings. Some of them were refugees for the second time, in fact, displaced. They had spent a long time in Srebrenica, in the enclave, being displaced from other places in Bosnia. They did not know what happened to their relatives, and many of them must have been in a state of shock. So when they were asked to give particulars about the missing persons, some, they did not always have the exact data. For example, date of birth is missing for a substantial -- exact date of birth is missing for a substantial number of persons. The year of birth is there for everybody but one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was the important data that you used in your study that came from the ICRC list?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The most important is, of course, the surname of the missing person; first name; and father's name, which is widely used in the former Yugoslavia, in the Balkans, to identify people; date of birth; place of birth; and not the least, place and date of disappearance; and also the opstina, the municipality of disappearance, with those data I had access to. The ICRC collected more data but these were the only data that were made public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did they take down ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, according to the questionnaire, they did that, but we never got access to that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were the missing from Srebrenica incorporated into the publication for all of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So in order to determine Srebrenica missing from the ICRC list, you have to put in certain data to determine who are actually missing from Srebrenica in 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So that's the ICRC list. Do you have any other observations about that list before we go onto the other list?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The total list, if you include everybody who has ever been reported, includes about 19.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And initially when you first got the volume, or what -- how many of those are related to Srebrenica, according to the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Some 7.400.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell us what you learned about the Physicians for Human Rights missing list. Who are they and what did you learn about them?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's an American-based, non-governmental organisation. I guess it's -- they're doing humanitarian work, human rights related work, and they wanted to assist particularly in identifying exhumed bodies related to Srebrenica. So in 1996, they started registering data on the missing persons much in the same way as ICRC did, but the objective was different. They wanted to use this information to identify people who were exhumed. So then in addition to asking the same questions as ICRC about place and date of disappearance, name, and so on, they also asked about particulars about the missing persons. For example, special physical characteristics, special clothing, special -- and something special about the teeth, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How long did that project continue?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I believe it continued until January this year when, apparently, they ran out of funds and it was taken over by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe who they took statements from? What kind of people did they allow to register?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Also close relatives. They were more -- they were more liberal, but also in their case was that -- were the missing persons reported by close relatives in more than 95 per cent of the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What about Srebrenica? Were they only Srebrenica or would they allow other people?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The main purpose was -- objective was to map Srebrenica, but they did not object to anybody coming in to report people going missing from other places. So of those 7.000-something, in their lists, in their database, about 80 per cent are Srebrenica-related.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you have access to the two volumes of the ICRC and the PHR lists in an electronic format?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. What was your next job, having access to these lists that you've described? What was the next job to meet your objective?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, first related to the ICRC lists, I have two different versions, so we had to merge those, making sure that nobody appeared twice. And also finding out if somebody was removed from version 3 to version 4, we needed to why were they removed; was it because they were found to be dead or found to be living.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So those that were found to be dead you would want to keep on your list, because that related to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: And we wanted, of course, to delete those found to be alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you go through that process?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. So we merged those two lists, and also together with a list of dead people published at the back of this book, about 600 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you do with the PHR list?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, also there we had different versions. We had to merge them, check for duplicates. We did not want the same person to be represented twice. It could be that some relatives went, actually, twice and were recorded by two different people or there was a mix-up in the data entry. And we did find some duplicates, and we checked with PHR later and they confirmed that we were right. So then we had two lists, one ICRC combined list, one PHR combined list. Then we merged those two lists. That was much more difficult, because most of the people appeared in both lists. So then we had to be very careful that we did not include people twice. We were conservative all the time, trying not to inflate the number but to get an exact and true picture of the number of missing as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just give us a brief idea of what was involved in the merging to --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, this was done using computers, of course, because of the large numbers, and we used the Access database programme and we searched for names that are equal; family name, first name, father's name, date of birth. If all those items are identical and place and date of disappearance are also similar or very similar, then we would accept this as being information for the same person. Now, a problem is that sometimes, as I told, the exact date of birth was missing. Then it was more difficult. Or there was misspellings in the names, and then we had to check this manually also to confirm that these were really the same people and not different people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you have another data source that helped you with that, the problems of misspellings and lack of information?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. We were fortunate in having a complete copy of the population census of 1991 for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what you learned about that, how reliable you believe that to be?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is a standard census which was -- it was taken then in 1991 in all of the former Yugoslavia, following similar censuses in 1981 and 1971 and so on. They record at the household level; also name, date of birth, ethnicity, in addition to lots of social variables like educational attainment, occupation, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is there a national ID number for people?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. A national ID number called maticni broj, meaning "unique number", was introduced in the former Yugoslavia in 1981. It consists of the date of birth, seven digits, and some additional six digits. But, if I may, this was recorded in the 1991 census, but not by everybody, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What were the problems with the 1991 census? I mean obviously 1991, in the former Yugoslavia, was not an easy time.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The major problem, I think, was that they did not have time to clean the data, as I said. The data was written on forms using longhand by enumerators and then entered into the computer by optical scanning. Now, depending on the handwriting of the enumerator, if the handwriting is poor, then there will be many mistakes introduced. And usually, this should be checked later, but because of the political problems that started at that time, they never had time to clean the data, clean and correct the data in the Bosnia census.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Be that as it may, it did provide another information source on particular names that might help you clear out difficulties as you've described in the other lists?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, and we believe it is very complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, that gets us back to the point where we have -- you've merged the ICRC list with the PHR list. However, we know from your testimony that the ICRC list contained people from the entire war and the PHR list contained some, I believe you said, 20 per cent non-related to Srebrenica. So how did you cull out from this big list the people that were just related to the Srebrenica incidents of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The investigation team of OTP told us that we should only include people who were reported as missing on the 11th of July or later and that we should only include people who went missing from places in or near Srebrenica or places related to the events. There were people who have very good knowledge about the events that happened in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the investigative team provided you with villages, and opstinas, and identification like that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about an ended date for gone missing? You mentioned July 11th as the beginning date. Was there an end date?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: 31st of August. However, we also included, I believe, 99 cases of people who went missing between the 1st of September and the 1st of December, because the places in which they went missing from were very related to the Srebrenica events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're referring to 1995 when you say "August"?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: 1995, yes. And we also included 68 cases of people who went missing in July 1995 but without known day of July. But other information shows that this was only true for half a per cent, so we are fairly safe to include those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: There were, of course, also people who went missing from Srebrenica before July 11th, but they were not included.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So were you able to, using those criteria and those lists, come up with a number, an initial number of total missing, after the fall of the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Based on both lists, we came up with a number of 7.490 who went missing from both -- from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what quality-control measures -- that's of course my term -- did you use to test the reliability of this number, 7.490?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, we looked at the data themselves to see if the age and sex structure of the data was consistent with what we had learned from other sources about the events, and that seemed to be the case, and we compared the data with other sources. The three major sources were the census of 1991, a list of voters who were listed in 1997, and also exhumed bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Was the list of voters one of the principle lists that you used to compare to your lists?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. There has been no post-war census in Bosnia, which would solve a lot of problems. The only comprehensive large-scale data collection activity has been undertaken by OSCE, that is, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe. That, as part of its mandate, is organising and supervising elections for democracy building, and they organised elections in 1996, 1997, 1998, and this year, 2000, and they established special registration procedures in 1997 and 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us, did you have access to the OSCE registration records of 1996, 1997, 1998?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: 1997 and 1998, yes. In 1996, there was no electoral register, so we didn't have access to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But there was elections?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. So then they used the 1991 census as the electoral register.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And so how did you deal with the two registration lists for 1997 and 1998?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, again we had to go through the same procedure, merge them, trying to avoid that the same people were included twice. There was a sequential number that helped us in doing that, but there were errors even there, some duplicates and some errors here and there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did OSCE ask people to put down their father's name?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Unfortunately not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there any other problems associated with the OSCE list like that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It was very limited information. They collected only a few items; surname, first name, date of birth, maticni broj, the ID number, and where the people lived in 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please be asked to slow down?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Sorry, I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You need to slow down.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Okay. And also where they were registered to vote, in which municipality, and which municipality they wanted to vote for. They did not collect any information on ethnicity, for example, and, as you said, not on father's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you find that many people in Bosnia had the same or similar names?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. There are some names that occur hundreds of times. The most common name in Bosnia is, I believe, "Fatima Hodzic". There are at least 500 persons by that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that presented some unique problems when comparing the OSCE voters registration lists to your missing lists?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, you can't do any comparison without more information on date of birth and, preferably, father's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Once you were able to merge the OSCE lists, what did you do in regard to the OSCE lists and your list, and why?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, we wanted to be absolutely sure that there were no people who were living amongst those 7.490 missing, so we matched that list, the missing list, with the voters' list, which consists of about 2.6 million records, to see if there were any living people, because that would make the missing list less reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you describe the process that you had to go through to match these very voluminous lists? I take it OSCE was also in electronic format.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. This should seem like an easy procedure if you have computers, and in a country like my own where data are almost perfect, we would have an ID number that is perfect, it would have been a very easy task. But again, because of lack of information or incomplete information in many fields, it was not so easy. Also, in the OSCE voters lists, there were misprints of names. They also used optical scanners, but the handwriting might have been better than the enumerator's 1991 handwriting. So there are a few errors. The maticni broj was also not recorded for everybody. That wouldn't have helped anyway, because that unique number is not represented in the missing persons' list. So we match on the basis of first name, last name, date of birth and opstina. That is all we actually could match. We tried different approaches. First we did that. Then -- and we got a long list. We looked at them. Then we tried, for example, to include only the initial of the last name, because of the misprints, and first name and date of birth, or only the year of birth, or the year of birth plus or minus one or plus or minus two, to try to eliminate -- to find as many possible or potential matches as possible. In fact, we came up with about 3.000 potential candidates. This was also done by the OSCE for the ICRC in Sarajevo. So altogether I think there were approximately 3.000 potential candidates of matches between the missing persons' list and the voters' list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you focus on those 3.000 potential matches to see if they were true matches or not?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. They were all inspected visually. Sometimes it was -- usually it was very obvious that these represented different persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you brought with you some examples of how you would have reviewed potential matches? I think it's Exhibit 278. It should be right there near the top.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Looking at Exhibit 278, could you -- there's a pointer there. Can you take us through that and explain the process that you looked at these 3.000 potential matches for?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. So what we got from the ICRC lists, we found a person -- there's a person by the name of Abdulah Delic. His father's name is Husein. Born in 1955. Then the computer, doing automatic searching, found a person by the same name, Abdulah Delic, born 1955, in the voters' registry in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. I notice the year of birth, all you've got here is "1955". Was that common, that you didn't have a month or a day?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It happened. Not so common. In the majority of the cases was the complete date of birth, but here I chose an example where that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Keep it as simple as possible. Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. And it also shows the ambiguities that we came across.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: So on the basis of this information, we could not tell -- we cannot tell whether these two records represent the same physical person. But then, fortunately, we had access to the census, and we looked up the census and we found two Abdulah Delics. The first person with a father Husein and the second whose father's Kemal. Moreover, the second person had the same maticni broj person who registered to vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's the ID number on the right of the column.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yeah, 183954. So we can quite safely conclude that these represent two different persons. It is one person, Abdulah Delic, who is registered as missing. There's another Abdulah Delic who registered to vote, but they're not the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this is an example of the kind of analysis that you did for all 3.000 of those potential matches?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were they all this easy?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Some were harder, but most were much easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The census you're talking about now, did that include all of Bosnia or was this a limited part of Bosnia that you were using?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The census was taken for all of Bosnia, but we made a census file including the seven opstinas in Eastern Bosnia surrounding Srebrenica to get a more manageable file.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Otherwise, you would have had many more Abdulah Delics?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. And the five consisted of somewhat more than 200.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you're considering that most of the missing went missing from Eastern Bosnia. Is that why that's a fair thing to do?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's what the investigation team has told you?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Actually, we checked that. Of a sample of people who went -- are on the missing list, 93 per cent went missing from Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you have another example of a true match?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you -- that is Exhibit 277. And can you explain that? And you can point out the actual things with your pointer, if you could.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Here on the ICRC list we have a man by the name Mensur Gabeljic. His father's name is Avdo. He was born in 1970. Then in the voters' register we found again Mensud but there was a misspelling. Sometimes the "LJ" is represented by a "Q," but this was corrected. So we found it. We discovered that. Without the father's name, because it's not recorded there, born on the 28th of 11, 1971. So here there are two inconsistencies. The "LJ" became "Q," which is very obvious. So that's not the problem really. Now, the ICRC person was born in 1970, the other in 1971, but as I said, there were -- sometimes the date -- should I speak slower? -- the year of birth was recorded slightly wrong. So we looked up the census, and we found only one person with this name or similar names, Gabeljic, his father was listed as Avoo, not Avdo, but that's a misprint, that's easy to understand, and he was born on exactly the same date as in the voters' register. Note that the maticni broj is missing in both of those sources. So here we conclude that these two names represent the same physical person. This is one of the nine people, although, the information has been changed to protect his identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I was going to ask you, after your analysis of the comparing the OSCE with the missing list you developed, how many matches or believe-to-be-true matches did you come up with?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I already said, nine matches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Like this one in this example?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Have you provided those matches to the investigative team for further investigation?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So what can you conclude from the results of the OSCE comparison to your missing list with nine matches, potential matches?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, it shouldn't be the case, of course, that missing people can vote or register to vote, so something is wrong. Either there was fraudulent registration of a missing person, there was fraudulent -- fraud in the registration of a voter, or -- those are two reasons. The third reason, that the missing person survived but does not want this known to the world, to relatives for various reasons, criminal, maybe he has remarried, you never know. There are a few cases like that. And the fourth is the mix-up of data. There is always errors in all data, so that is the other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this is the kind of thing that the investigative team will be able to sort out?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So nine potential matches out of all these thousands of names. What does that do, in your opinion, to the reliability of the 7.400-plus names?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: In my opinion, this is insignificant. Out of almost 7.500, nine people, that is approximately one-tenth of a per cent, and it is insignificant compared to the large number. So it shows that -- it indicates -- it is not proof, of course, but it's a strong indication that the missing persons are dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can we go to Exhibit 272, where I think you lay this out very clearly, and if you could just explain each of the columns and the numbers.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. After this merging procedure of different files on missing persons, we found that 5.712 people came -- were registered both by ICRC and PHR. So the majority were registered by both agencies. In addition, there were 1.586 people registered by ICRC only and 192 registered by PHR only, adding up to 7.490, as explained previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So with all of PHR's work, they only registered 192 more than ICRC did?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. And this is an indication that the coverage of ICRC was very good and surprisingly good, since PHR used different methods and in a more -- in a less turbulent period. So you should think that people should be more willing to come forward, but also PHR had a lack of resources and could not collect that data all over Bosnia and not abroad, as ICRC also did. So it resulted only in 192 additional missing people, although this was not the primary person to -- reason for them to collect data on additional people but to get more information on everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So that leaves us with the 7.490 that we've been talking about. Then what's the next column?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Then we had, to be on the safe side, to be sure, we subtract the nine inconsistent cases that we talked about. Those that were found -- also found in the voters' register. The number may be lower but it is nine at the most. So we end up with 7.481 missing people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what's the next column about?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Then we asked the ICRC if they could provide us with the names of those who were taken off the lists of missing persons after January 1997 because they were found to be alive, and they that said they cannot do that, they will not reveal their identities, but we were told that there were six related cases like that. So we have subtracted those. We don't know their identities, but we know there that are six people. So we subtract that, to be on the safe side. Those six could actually also be -- could be some of the same as those nine, actually. It could be that -- it's very likely that they are included in the nine, but we don't know. So we end up with 7.475 missing people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are those people and their names listed in what is Exhibit 271?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you just hold that up so we could see what that is?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that's the other exhibit.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this is the published list that the ICTY or the OTP has done reflecting your research?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I notice that it includes 7.481 names because of those six names. We don't know their identities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you've stated earlier that the ICRC didn't take ethnicity down. So there must have been a significant number of the missing where you don't have ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, but the PHR took that down, and of the 5.556 coming from the PHR list, there were 5.555 Bosniaks or Muslims and 1 Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So how many does that leave left over from ICRC that you don't have a record for?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: One thousand nine hundred and twenty-five. Then we looked at the names of those people, and we compared the names of these with the census and found that there were probably around four additional -- three or four additional non-Muslims, one Yugoslav, one Croat, one Serb, and one with unstated ethnicity or something. So that leaves us with a total of five non-Muslims of those 7.481 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So how did you account for those non-Muslim names?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Why that would happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, this could be due to many causes. Intermarriage is one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you choose to subtract those from the list?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You've discussed a couple of other things you did for quality control of those numbers, and I think you've got some exhibits that illustrate that. You can put those on please. Tell us what exhibit.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: This is Exhibit 273. I think this could be enlarged a little bit. This shows the age distribution of the men who went missing from Srebrenica, and we see that the most common -- yeah, that's better. The most common age group is around 18, 19, 20, where more than 250 of that age went missing. The youngest here is 14, two 14-year-olds. The oldest here is 89.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As a demographer, how does this support the quality of the list? Why isn't it just a reflection of what the list tells you?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, we can look at the age structure here. It is a bit jagged, there are peaks here, but probably not more than you would expect of a small population like this where this sampling varies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What is it about this figure that supports the validity of the lists?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It is consistent with the reports that we have heard, that there were mostly young men who were separated from their families and who were reported as missing, and that it's a reasonably smooth age structure. Not perfect. That could also be due to errors in the age reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you mean by smooth age structure?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why would we expect a smooth age structure?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, we wouldn't expect many more 30-year-olds missing than 29-year-olds and 31-year-olds. So approximately the same. This trough here around age 50 is probably due to lower number of births during the Second World War, so there are fewer people in that age group, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Why don't we go to the next exhibit. I believe it's -- well, whichever one you want to use.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: 275 -- no, 274. More on the age structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, this exhibit actually gives us the number of the various ages. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yeah. It shows us first that there were -- most of the people who are on the missing list are men. There are only 48 women on the list of missing persons and 2.433 men. It also shows us is that there are a significant number of young and old men; 199 below the age of 17, which is normally believed to be the military -- lowest military age. The youngest men were, sorry, not 14 but 13. The youngest women were two girls aged 8. There's also a high number of old people, aged 60 and above, or 739.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was this chart something that the Prosecution specifically asked you to do to illustrate the actual ages?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Partly, but as a demographer, it's very natural to produce tables by age and sex.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You can go to the next exhibit. Exhibit 275. What is this?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Here we have compared the age distribution of the missing persons with the age distribution of the exhumed bodies. There are very few bodies that have been identified, only around 70 so far. So these are the -- the red ones -- red bars show the -- show the age distribution of the -- approximately 1.900 exhumed bodies where the ages or age ranges have been estimated using methods that you have heard about during the last days. The blue bars represent the age distribution of the missing persons, the 7.481 missing persons on the list. We see -- so that the age distributions are fairly similar. Not surprisingly similar but they are very similar. This indicates that the exhumed bodies come from the population of missing persons, that they represent the same population, you could say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How could you account for the differences?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: There are two causes of differences. The most important is that estimating age on the basis of bone fragments is not an exact science. This was elaborated, I believe, over the last couple of days. Secondly, the sampling variability. So when you draw a sample, here of 1.900 from more than 7.000, you are bound to get some sampling variations, some errors in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You had 1.900. That's about the number of bodies recovered that the anthropologists worked with.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, in addition to that work, did the investigation present you with certain published challenges to the credibility of the ICRC list?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. We received four examples of that from Belgrade sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you turn to page 9 in your report where I think you outline those challenges and you discuss them, and if you could put page 9 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I think we can focus on the top one first. Yes, like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So the one that's entitled "Lacking the Date of Birth," where did that come from as far as you know, based on what you were given, this particular challenge?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It came from the Law Project Centre in Yugoslavia, as specified in footnote 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know anything about who or what that is?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was just provided to you by the investigation?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was that particular challenge?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I can read. It was -- it says that for 60 per cent of the people from the list there is no information such as date of birth, which is quite impossible, for they have been reported missing by their closest family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: First -- at first glance, this seems like a very reasonable allegation, I agree. Now, when we looked at this more closely, we saw that it was not quite true, that claim, since the year of birth is missing for nobody -- or for only one person, and month of birth is missing 44 per cent, and day of birth for 46 per cent. So the real -- it is complete, the date of birth is complete for 53.5 per cent of the population. So less than claimed here. I don't know where date of birth, what they mean, whether they mean complete date of birth or year of birth. We can interpret it as being complete date of birth and then the true figure should be 53.5 per cent. And as I indicated earlier, it is not at all surprising that the relatives and the informants did not have exact information on the exact date of birth of the missing persons, because the identification papers and other documents of these people were carried by the people who had disappeared. So they did not have access to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Still, these numbers of lack of specificity of date of birth, does that make your work invalid or --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Let me also add that it is very common in many cultures not to put so much attention on the exact date of birth. I think in our culture in Western Europe and the United States, we are more concerned about the date of birth, and in some other cultures, where, for example, a father's name is a more important piece of identification. And also many of the people who informed the ICRC and PHR were old and did not remember exactly the exact date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did this cripple your analysis?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Not at all, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next challenge. Could you again, I think, just read it and --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. "On the list of 3.016 missing persons officially recorded in the registers of the International Red Cross, the names of 350 persons whose identity has been established with certainty appear on the electoral list of September 1996."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So they are saying that the voters' registration -- in their comparison of the voters' registration to the ICRC, they come up with 350 matches. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated, there was no voters' register in 1996. The voters' register was this census of 1991. So it is not at all surprising that people who went missing in 1995 were on the lists recorded in 1991. They should be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But if basically you're saying they compared the census to the census, why is there only 350 --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Sorry, not the census to the census but the missing to the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The missing to the census. Why is there only 350?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, in the electoral, they said they had only compared names beginning with the letters "A" and "K", which is slightly more than half of the alphabet when you're thinking of persons with those names, and they only compared named with complete information on both lists. That's complete name and complete date of birth. Now, that is about half on each. One half times one half is a quarter. If you then multiply by there one half of the alphabet that was included, you get about one-eighth. One-eighth of 3.000 is approximately 350, so that would be the expected number of matches -- no, 360, and that would be the expected number of matches to be found in such an exercise, and they found 350.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you went through the same exercise they did and came up with the same number?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, this was just estimating the probability that they would find, the expected number of matches they would find, and I came up with approximately the same number as they actually found.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you again explain to me why that is invalid again?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Because they did not find any -- this is no claim that living -- they claim that -- excuse me -- that there were missing persons who registered to vote by comparing the missing persons and what they said was the voting lists. But there was no voting list. It was the census they compared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: People that were counted in 1991?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: And of course most of them would be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next one down, the next challenge.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: In the book "Radovan Karadzic", it is claimed that several persons reported as missing on the ICRC list also appear on the voters' lists, and they list 17 persons by name, picked by random, related to men from Srebrenica. We found 11 of those names on the voters' lists, but when we checked the date of birth and ID number with our census records, these were not true matches. So they were false matches. So their names were similar, but the dates of birth were not similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You went through the process that you already have described to us. You're able to exclude those names?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go down to the last one in your report.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It was also claimed that many people were listed as missing who died before 1995 from natural causes or in combat, and they gave a list of names and dates of birth taken from a cemetery in Kazani of people who died between 1992 and early 1995. But when we looked at the ICRC lists, we did not find any of those names with the same date of birth or approximately the same date of birth as alleged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, very recently has the investigation provided you with another challenge to the credibility that the investigation has received, very similar to this last one regarding people dead prior to the fall?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. The Office of the Prosecutor has received lists originating from the Bosnian army, the BiH army, of soldiers who were either killed, wounded, captured, or missing in action before July 1995, some in 1994. And the total of this list include 1.139 names of soldiers then, and they disclaim that these people are registered as missing, although they died -- many of them died before July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you, in the last couple of days, been able to make an attempt to analyse this information?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. The problem is that some of the data is very deficient. But for one list of 242 people, date of birth is given, and we compared it with the list of missing persons, a number found. So none of those 242 dead and/or captured or wounded soldiers have been reported as missing. In addition, there were then eight, nine hundred people we checked, but they without date of birth. So it was only the name, only first name and last name. This is very hard to identify. We found 188 of these names on the list of missing persons based on only first name and last name, but that does not necessarily mean that these are registered as missing, because some of these names are very common. Some of these names occur 26 times in the census of Eastern Bosnia in 1991. So we cannot be sure that that name found here in this list by first name and last name does not mean -- necessarily mean that it represents one of these dead soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you able to narrow down that number, one hundred and -- what did you say it was?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: One eighty-eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- 188 at all?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. We found -- for 183 of those, we found more than one occurrence of the name in the census, so it means that there could be -- there are more people, there are more Mehemed Hodzics than the one reported -- than the dead soldier in the lists. For five people, we found only one, but the investigations are continuing, and it could be that some of these registered were enumerated outside Eastern Bosnia in 1991, and we are currently looking into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did I ask you this morning just to analyse how many people went missing from Potocari according to your lists?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I believe there are 2.380 or 2.280, something like that. But that includes also some -- includes many people who were later seen elsewhere -- 2.280, yes -- because they could be reported as missing from Potocari to the ICRC and missing from elsewhere to PHR. But 2.280.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we've been talking about missing lists. Did you, in your report, discuss the issue of whether these missing were, in fact, truly missing or were probably dead?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, our analysis indicated that they are dead, as we have found very few potential examples of survivors. I mention nine and those six from ICRC. That is a maximum of 15. We have checked -- compared with various lists, and they do not seem to be many, if any, survivors. We also looked at a list of 70 exhumed bodies who were identified, and we found -- on that list, we found 66 people who were also on the missing lists. Then there were two who are missing in the Srebrenica-related graves, but they were not on the lists so they have not been reported as missing, and two who went missing before July 1995. So that's a fairly high percentage of people who are known to be dead but who are also on the missing lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You mentioned people that have been identified. Now, is that -- what organisation is attempting the identifications?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It's something called the Podrinje Identification Project, and also the PHR are working on or were working on identifying people, in addition to the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, can you conclude with the summary of why you believe that the total number, 7.433, is a reliable number, and tell us whether or not it's a conservative number.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I think it's quite reliable or very reliable and that it is a minimum estimate of all of the number of missing persons. We have been very conservative, very cautious, tried to avoid including duplicates or avoiding other errors, and we have deleted actually a number of cases which could be included. Several hundred cases have been excluded because there was some inconsistency between the information reported to ICRC and to PHR; for example, on the date of birth or place of disappearance. But it is likely that some of these several hundred are also missing from Srebrenica. In addition, we believe that there are quite a few people who did not report their relatives as missing, as we just mentioned an example of two persons. That could be many reasons. One is that the whole family disappeared. Others have given -- families have given up all hope of seeing these relatives again. Remember that this is a part of a tracing exercise, tracing operation, so the purpose for people to trace -- record people as missing was to be united with their families, to trace them, to find out what happened, not really to come up with an aggregate number of missing people. I don't think that was in people's minds. So a combination, and some people were obviously sick, or mental problems, or there were many reasons why everybody would not report a person as missing. But 7.475 should be considered a minimum number, a conservative number. The actual number is probably higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that fundamentally, the credibility of these lists is founded upon the Bosnian families that made the reporting to the various institutions?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, but not only, because we have checked with other data sources and we have found that all the data that they reported are true. These are not made-up persons, they are not phantom persons, because almost whenever we tried to find a person in the census, 1991 census, we found him or her, as I said, in 93 per cent of the cases. And it could be that those seven additional per cent were enumerated elsewhere in Bosnia, not in Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. I think this is a convenient time for a break. We will have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Brunborg, you are now going to answer questions which I see Mr. Petrusic, Defence attorney, is going to ask you. Mr. Petrusic, you have the floor. You may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, my learned friends from the Prosecution; and good morning, Mr. Brunborg.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: My first question is a general one, and that is, regarding your report on the number of dead and missing in Srebrenica, of the 12th of February, 2000, the list of the missing, is that a component part of your report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I think it should be considered an addendum to the report or an appendix, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 2 of your report, you talk about the methods used in your study, and one of the methods is the evaluation of the quality of data sources, particularly those regarding missing persons. Did you or your associates in this project check the quality of the data sources?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. We looked carefully at all the data collected. We also talked to representatives of the ICRC in Sarajevo. We started a questionnaire, and we evaluated each field recorded, the names, date of birth, father's name, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: As far as I am able to understand from your answer, your direct contacts were with representatives of the International Red Cross, if we're talking about their list.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Representatives of that organisation or the Physicians for Human Rights who compiled those lists in the way you have described, they collected those data on the basis of direct contacts with relatives who reported their missing members, family members.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you or the representatives of your team have any direct contact to check the allegations made by relatives who reported their family members as missing?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. Let me first say that we also met several times with the representatives of the Physicians for Human Rights, and we also met with some relatives of missing persons who had reported their relatives as missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So this was a limited number of people that you or members of your team had contact with among the relatives?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. We did not have the capacity to meet a large number of those 7.500 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Page 8 of your report, you discuss the age group of the missing people from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The Defence was not able to review your list for technical reasons, because it was just prior to the beginning of today's hearing that we received the list, but a very superficial review of that list shows that a very large number of people have their date of birth indicated.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: My question is, in that connection, whether the table that you have given, that is table number 2, could it have been more precise regarding the able structure in view of the fact that for a very large number of people the date of birth is given in the list, especially the people in the age group between 15 to 60 or 16 to 60?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No. This list was available, of course, finished before the 12th of July, and the day -- the year of birth is recorded for everybody but one person. So that decides the age. So we know that age for everybody but one, and this is also indicated in table 2," Men, age unkown". There's only one person. The dates of birth reported in the list is taken either from the ICRC list or from the PHR lists, depending on whether it appeared. If it is missing from the ICRC list, it's taken from the PHR list and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But the range from 16 to 60 as an age group, couldn't it have been narrowed down, broken down into two or three groups within that age range?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Definitely, that's possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brunborg, on page 12 of your report -- in the English version it may be page 11 -- you refer to the number of 1.909. Page 11 of the English version. I beg your pardon. The number of people found in mass graves is 1.909?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The team of experts, including anthropologists, in their study and report give the figure of 1.883 persons. When compiling this list and compiling these numbers, including the one I have referred to regarding dead bodies found so far of 1.909, did you bear in mind the reports issued by the pathologists and anthropologists regarding the same issue?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: My figure is based on report dated December 8 last year, when we -- when I wrote my report, and the most recent anthropological report had not been available to me. But the number of exhumed bodies has changed a little bit, I notice. I don't know the reasons for that. It could be that it is often based on fragments of bodies and it is difficult to give exact estimates. Anyway, it is close to 1.900.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In your report, when you referred to defining the term of victims from Srebrenica -- this is on page 3 and "Definition of Terms" is the heading -- you talk about the place of disappearance, among other things. In view of the fact that the term "when a person was last seen" is used, could it be possible for a person to be reported as missing twice and maybe more times because it may have been seen for the last time by a certain group of people in several places? You have given an example here of a person who may have been seen for the last time in Nova Kasaba, or Srebrenica, I'm sorry, and after that in Zume or Nova Kasaba, in the forest or in Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, let me answer. For more than 5.700 people were reported twice, both by the -- that is, both by the ICRC and by PHR, so they reported twice. And as I explained, we took great care, when merging the lists, to avoid keeping such person for more than once. It should not be -- deleting duplicates. We also found some duplicates in the ICRC lists and in the PHR lists on the basis of name, date of birth, and other information, and we deleted such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Towards the end, you also speak about the unique identification number of citizens established in the territory of the former Yugoslavia and that that national ID number was used as an element for identification in the census of 1991. You said that it provoked a lot of -- that it had many imprecisions because of the way in which the enumerators registered the data they collected. Mr. Brunborg, this national ID number was established in the territory of the former Yugoslavia in 1981, so in the census of 1991 it was already -- it was being used for the second time, so it had been tested in practice. In view of that being a unique national ID number, could it have been a more reliable element to be used in the course of your studies?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Now, I checked the maticni broj for those people from the Srebrenica area, those seven municipalities, and it appears to be correct for two thirds of the cases; 67 per cent, it is absolutely correct. So it means that it is incorrect or, I would say, partly missing or -- for one third. In the voters' register in 1997, it appears to be correct for more than 80 per cent of those cases. I believe that the number was used not only in the census, 1991, but was also used for other purposes, so that many people had some experience using the number and they knew the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions. Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. McCloskey, have you any re-examination for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. Judge Fouad Riad, if you please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [In English] Mr. Brunborg, good morning.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just have two global questions, not being a great expert like you. You mentioned that according to your analysis, you reached the conclusion that the missing persons would be either 7.475 or 7.481, whatever the number is. According to your long experience, what could be the margin of inaccuracies in such analysis?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is a very difficult answer to question [sic], Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Would it be just in the number, whether instead of being 7.000 it could be 6.000, or would it be in the totality?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No. I think that this is very close to the lower number. It is a minimum estimate. And I do not believe that the real number can be much lower than 7.475. Maybe a handful or two, but very few. But it could be considerably higher. So the range of uncertainty is very little, on the low side, but it is -- it could extend by several hundred, at least, upwards, because, as I said, we have been very conservative and excluded all cases where we were in doubt about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That's good to know. My second question: You mentioned that -- because perhaps it's related to this answer, you said that everybody did not report missing persons and perhaps you consider that the number must have been higher, and you affirmed it as a fact. Do you have any evidence that some people really did not report, or is it your logical conclusion according to your experience?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is mentioned in the report that two people who were identified bodies found in a grave with other -- with Srebrenica-related bodies were not on the list. So there we have an example of two dead people who went missing from Srebrenica. They're reported as missing and then also found in a grave. So those are examples of people not included in our list, not reported as missing. It could be that they were reported as missing but with insufficient information, unclear information for us to include them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That was the only perhaps example of people not reported or some people in your contacts expressed the fact that they don't care to report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I don't remember that we met such persons, but we met -- we asked whether people knew about whole families that were not reported, and we learned about a couple of cases of such family. Names of such families were mentioned. One of those families were indeed reported, where whole families had disappeared, and the other family was not reported. So there are such cases. But we did not have the capacity to do a lot of work, to trace people who did not report -- were not reported as missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Brunborg.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad. Madam Judge Wald, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Professor Brunborg, was any attempt made to take into consideration whether or not people, during these turbulent times, who were reported as missing might eventually have left the entire country of Bosnia? We have had many witnesses who have come back from other countries. Would there be any way of knowing if that happened?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
