utterances.text: We did not know where the people were registered as missing, but I believe that it was possible to do that all over the world, either to local ICRC offices or perhaps there was a mail system. I'm not aware how that was done, but I know there were people registered as missing in other countries by refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So that if, if supposedly one of the missing people here eventually survived and later emigrated to some neighbouring country, there was some possibility or likelihood that that would be reported back to the ICRC so that they take them off the missing list?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. If such a person has relatives who reported that person as missing or know somebody else who know that his name is on the list, they will probably report to the ICRC, but I don't think there is an automatic mechanism for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That was my next question.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You told us a little bit about the intake methods of the ICRC, the relatives or close -- relatives making reports. Is there any organised method by which the ICRC receives reports that people who are originally reported as missing later have been found and -- I mean do they have a regular system? Do they ask the people who originally report to let them know if the person turns up or is that just up to chance?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I don't know -- I do not know the system in detail, but many people are taken off the lists, several hundred between the different versions. ICRC has regular meetings in Sarajevo with the three parties involved in the armed conflict and they exchange information. When they learn about a death either through exhumations or otherwise, that person is taken off the list. Likewise, I believe that when they learn about a person who is alive and not dead, they will take that person off the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My third question relates to the volume of Srebrenica missing. You touched on this a little bit in your testimony on cross-examination, the fact that under the column "Date and Place of Disappearance," in many cases -- this is a general question -- in many cases, the place of disappearance may not be Srebrenica or Potocari but will be Bratunac or Zvornik, one of those places that is in the immediate area and that has been involved in the exodus from Srebrenica. But my question specifically is: Before somebody gets on this list, what kind of a link to the exodus from Srebrenica is necessary? Does the relative have to say, "He used to live in Srebrenica," or, "He was part of the exodus"? How would you avoid getting somebody, say, who lived in Bratunac or was killed in some little combat thing in Bratunac? How do you link that -- people who have a different location in that column to the whole Srebrenica exodus?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Your Honour, the PHR asked -- had a specific question on whether the person went missing after the fall of the enclave, relative to that fall. So that's a specific question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: How about the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: They did not have a specific question, but they say that often the person reported would say that, volunteer that information. However, we did not have access to that information, so we decided whether it was related to the fall of Srebrenica through the place of disappearance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And the time.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: And the time. The places of disappearance were provided to us by the investigators and people knowledgeable about this. Some of the place names on these lists are very small, very small places. Most of the places can be found on the map. When they cannot be found on the map, we went to local people and asked, "Where is this place?" We did not ask them -- tell them why we asked this question, "Could you tell us where is this place?" They pointed to the map and saw this was a small hamlet or something. When that was related to the exodus or the events in Srebrenica it was included, otherwise, not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Professor Brunborg, I have five very brief questions for you, and in a way, all of my questions are of a general nature. You have told us that for a demographer, age and sex are two main criteria in research. What was the role and what would be your conclusions -- your conclusions in connection with that of the military age?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Now, women are not considered to be of military age. We can keep those out. I have been told that as shown in one of the exhibits, that the military ages are between, say, 16 and 60. Now, after more detailed discussions with people knowledgeable about that, I included in the Exhibit 274, 17 through 59 -- sorry, 17 as the lower age. People are drafted as age 18 but they can be registered as soldiers from age 17. When they turn 60, they are not part of the -- cannot be considered part of the armed forces any more. So that's why it's 59 inclusive and 17 inclusive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My second question for you, Professor, is the following, it is a follow-up to my first question, actually: On page 8 of your report you have table number 2. I told you it's probably a follow-up to my first question, but I should like to know what were the criteria to establish age groups that are indicated in this table? Was the military age taken into account or was it the case where another criterion was applied?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: These are the military ages as told to me half a year ago, but then after a more -- as I said, thorough discussions, I decided to include 17 through 59. There are not so many people in those age group. There are 104 or something 16-year-old men and a similar number or a little bit lower of 60-year-old men. So it does not affect the results very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your report, you make mention of the Exhibit number 275. It is a table that shows age distribution of missing persons together with exhumed bodies. Yes. This is the one that I'm referring to. I don't know whether you have spoken about it, and I apologise if this was the case, but I should like to know why the number of exhumations is higher than the number of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The total number is not higher, Your Honour. It is 1.900 versus 7.481. It is true that it is slightly higher in one age group, the youngest, 8 through 12, where we have only recorded two missing persons, two men 13 years old, whereas there were exhumed six or seven bodies in that age group. But as you heard yesterday and the day before, it is very difficult to estimate those ages and it could very well be that some of the 13- and 14-year-olds were wrongly classified as belonging to the youngest age group, 8 to 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You spoke about contacts that you had with families who provided you with the information. Why did you make those contacts? I do not wish to lead you in any way, but could you tell me, what was the reason of those contacts with families?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The major reason was to find out about the interview situation; what happened, how did they react to it, what did they think about it. I did not use those contacts to gather information on more missing persons, just to get some feeling for how they reacted in that situation. And I would say they were not always positive. They felt sometimes they were treated not very well, treated impolitely by some other organisations. And this should be seen in the light of the very traumatic situation they were experiencing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's say that it was a humane reason. You did not contact the families in order to test the reliability of the information or in order to resolve a specific problem; you did it for, if I may say so, humanitarian reasons?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Not really. Just to understand more about the process. The data were checked not with the families but with the census 1991, where the persons themselves came forward with information. So we thought that was a more reliable source and also a more comprehensive source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me finish, Professor, with another question I think you spoke about. To what extent can we say that missing people equals dead people?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Now, of course, ordinarily to declare that a person is dead requires either a -- in statistics, requires a medical certificate or, if that cannot be obtained, by a certificate provided by a judge. So there should be medical or legal evidence that a person is dead, and we do not have that for these people because most of the bodies have not been found and there is a lack of witnesses. So we cannot be sure, but all indications -- all these investigations and analyses point in one direction, that the people are dead, supposed to be dead. There are also some people we know to be dead amongst these and, as I said, at the most 15 people of them may be alive; probably less. So I think comparing with all kinds of sources, with the voters' register and exhumed bodies and otherwise, they all indicate that these people are dead. Let me also add that the ICRC has repeatedly visited prisons in Serbia because of claims that many of these missing people are in detention in Serbia and elsewhere, and they did find some at the beginning, who were then taken off the lists, but recently -- my understanding is that in recent years, they haven't found anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Professor. I think that we have to take care of the exhibits that have been tendered. Mr. McCloskey, I believe that you wish to tender some exhibits at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Those exhibits are number 269, the CV, resume; 270, the ICRC report; 271, the ICTY compilation report; 272; 273; 274; 275, which are some of the charts, I believe; 276, which is the missing reports, 276A and B, which are in Bosnian and French; 277 and 278.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has one general objection in respect of Exhibits 271 and 270. The reason of our objection is that we received all of the exhibits only today. But these two exhibits are quite voluminous. It is an appendix to the report composed by Mr. Brunborg. The other exhibit, number 270, is a report of the ICRC in connection with missing persons from that area. The Defence simply was not in a position to verify the allegations made in these two exhibits because of the method of a random sample that was used. So we should like to ask the Trial Chamber to give us some additional time to present our arguments regarding these two exhibits. As regards other exhibits that have been tendered by the Prosecutor, we do not have any objections, although they are in close connection with the two exhibits we object to. However, in view of the fact that they are of a statistical nature, we will accept them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I would point out that the Defence has had Mr. Brunborg's report, and I don't know the exact date, but since April. The references to the source material are very clear in that report. The ICRC missing list is a publication that can be acquired everywhere, especially in the former Yugoslavia, and we have never received a request to obtain the list otherwise, which would amount to, I believe it was, 182 additional names that the ICRC list did not have until right now. Having said that, if counsel needs more time to review it, I don't believe we have any objection to that and understand the situation they are in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Mr. Petrusic, do you wish to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, only in order to avoid confusion. Mr. McCloskey is referring to the report. It is true that we received it, and we used it for cross-examination. However, as regards Exhibit 271 which is being tendered, it is in respect of that document that we raise an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. I will consult my colleagues. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber will admit all of the exhibits that have been tendered. As regards to exhibits 270 and 271, we will grant additional time to the Defence to review or verify the data that are contained therein. Mr. Petrusic, I don't think that you will need more than one month to do that. Is one month enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, do you agree with this additional time, one additional month for the Defence to review the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the Chamber grants additional time, one month, for the Defence to review the documents. All other exhibits have been admitted into evidence. Professor Brunborg, we have finished with your testimony. Thank you very much once again for coming here to testify. Thank you for your cooperation, and you have accomplished very valuable work here. Thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see Mr. Harmon coming to take the floor, but Mr. Visnjic is also standing. Perhaps I should give the floor to him first. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I may take five minutes of the Court's time in order to follow up on the situation that has been raised just recently. We have noticed a problem here which might have significance in terms of the disclosure process as regards expert witness reports. The position adopted by the Defence is as follows: If the documents are significant for the testimony, or if the documents are a component part of the report of the expert witness, then in that case such documentation, such evidence, should be disclosed or made available to the Defence at the same time as the expert witness report, in accordance with Rule 94 bis. Let me state two examples in support of this submission. We have just seen one example. One of the main reasons why the Defence has used, in terms of cross-examination, was the fact that the list of missing persons was not addended [sic] to the report, it was not annexed to the report of the expert witness that has just testified here, so we were not in a position to check his allegations. On the other hand, on the 18th of May, in accordance with Rule 94 bis A, the Prosecutor submitted a report to the Court in connection to a specific document. When we received the report, we realised that the said document had not been disclosed to us, and we were not in a position to make submissions on something that we did not see at all. So we contacted the Prosecution in respect of that, and upon our request, the Prosecutor has made it available to us, the said document which was subject of the expert witness analysis. That document would probably be accepted by us without even using our right to cross-examination. In that sense, we believe -- it is our position that in addition to each expert witness report tendered by the Prosecutor in accordance with Rule 94 bis, additional evidence should also be disclosed, namely, evidence that is also part of that testimony or, rather, the expert witness report. In case of delay, in case an expert witness report is disclosed first and additional documents are disclosed only later on, in that case we believe that we should be given an opportunity -- and this should, of course, apply to the Prosecutor during the Defence case -- that the time limits stated in Rule 94 bis, namely, the 14-day deadline, should be extended, taking into account the delay that has elapsed. So we should like to hear the Chamber. We should like to hear the position of the Chamber in respect to this issue in order to avoid any future misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, before answering the question raised by Mr. Visnjic, I should like to ask you first, do you have other witnesses or other experts to call and bring into the courtroom for today and tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, we do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we know then what we're going to do afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In respect of today's hearing, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Today we will have a videotape of testimony that was taken in 1996 from a gentleman, Mr. Pasaga Mesic, that was given in the Rule 61 hearing, in the Karadzic and Mladic Rule 61 hearing. It's approximately 29 minutes long. We're going to tender that as our next piece of evidence. Thereafter, I intend to introduce an expert report that has been consented to by the Defence. It is the expert report of Mark Mills, who is an expert on watches. Thereafter, I have a series of documents that I will be tendering to the Court. And at some point today, I've been informed by the Defence that they want to cross-examine Mr. Manning, whose cross-examination has been deferred. We will ask Mr. Manning to come back into the courtroom and be available for cross-examination by the Defence and Your Honours' questions and any redirect examination by the Prosecutor, and that concludes today's session, if we can get through all of that. I would need to go into a private session, perhaps, in respect of the remainder of the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked you this because I should like to make a distinction between the hearing time when we have witnesses and experts waiting and matters relating to the organisation of work, which we can leave for another time, specifically the afternoon. But I think now we can hear Mr. Harmon's response to the questions asked by Mr. Visnjic, which doesn't mean that next time we can have a Status Conference in the afternoon to discuss these matters to avoid witnesses waiting. I wish to have this distinction and avoid discussing organisational matters during the time reserved for hearings, making the witnesses wait, sometimes over the weekend. If we make this distinction, then we have guaranteed time to hear the witnesses and to discuss organisational matters in the afternoon. Mr. Harmon, can we have your response, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel. The issue raised by my colleague is one that I think should have additional reflection, additional time to discuss amongst the parties to this litigation. However, let me respond, at least in the beginning, by saying under the Rule, which is 94 bis, the requirement under 94 bis (A) requires the full statement of any expert witness, and in many cases it clearly does not state the full statement and all supporting documentation. Now, I think Rule 94 bis has to be read in context with the other Rules. The other Rules -- let me say, it has to be read in context with the other Rules so as not to eviscerate other important rules in this set of comprehensive rules. Let me give you an example. Under Rule 66(B): "The Prosecutor shall, upon request, permit the Defence to inspect any books, documents, photographs, and tangible objects in the Prosecutor's custody or control which are material to the preparation of the defence or are intended for use by the Prosecutor as evidence at trial or were obtained from or belong to the accused." Now, what this Rule clearly says is if the Defence wants to see those kinds of documents, they have to make a request. And there's a quid pro quo. The quid pro quo is found in the reciprocal discovery provision found in Rule 67(C). If they make the request, then the Prosecutor, likewise, is able to examine all of the material that the Defence -- any books, documents, photographs, and tangible objects which are in their control and which they intend to use as evidence at trial. Conceivably, an interpretation of Rule 94 bis as suggested by the Defence, which asked for not only the statement of the expert but all the supporting documentation, can drive a hole through this balance that is found presently in these Rules. For example, if the Prosecutor intends to call an expert that deals with the central elements of this case and in support of that expert would submit, eventually as pieces of evidence, a hundred documents, by making the request that my colleague has made, not only to see the statement but, in addition, all the documents that support the witness, you will have the consequence of eviscerating the reciprocal discovery provisions. So it is our position that under Rule 94 bis, the testimony of an expert witness, these witnesses have prepared statements, those statements have been produced, but it's our position that the Defence is not entitled to see all of the documents that support those expert statements because they have to make a request to see those under 67. That's the position that we take. We've invited the Defence, on many occasions -- I've informed them in writing and orally, that we intend to produce many documents, a large volume of documents in the upcoming sessions of this proceeding. I've invited them to inspect those documents if they're willing to make a request under the Rule 67, and we'll make them available, and the Defence has explicitly declined both my oral request and my written request. So our view is one has to read the Rules in their entirety, and our interpretation of these Rules in their entirety favour a balance, a balance that can be seen by providing the statement of the expert to the Defence, the Defence can consult with their own experts based on the statement of the expert, but to entitle them to see all of the supporting material behind that is, in our view, something that creates an imbalance and could the purpose and effect of the other Rules in the whole scheme. So that's our position. I think this issue may bear additional reflection, but that's my initial reaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, you are entitled to a response.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has given thought to the submission made by Mr. Harmon, so we would have a brief response to it. Within the framework of the complete set of Rules, one of the Rules envisaged is the Rule that the accused must be entitled to a timely defence. In the conviction of the Defence, the Prosecutor must, at a certain point of time, disclose all of the documents and submit them to the Trial Chamber and thereby also to the Defence. Now if we would reduce the matter to procedural economy. Let us assume that the Prosecutor has an expert witness to whose testimony they wish to attach about a hundred documents which are of substantive importance for the trial. In that case, if these are indeed important documents and the Defence did not have a chance to verify them, we assume that the Defence will most probably object to those documents, in which case again, in light of all the other Rules, it would be granted additional time from the time those documents were disclosed, additional time to review those documents, and then that would mean bringing back the expert at least on one other occasion. I do not think that the right of the Prosecution to disclose of documents as envisaged under 66(B), that is, rather, retaining those documents, would be at risk if those documents were to be disclosed only 21 days in advance, at the same time as the expert report, in other words. In that case, the Defence would have sufficient time, or we can assume it would have sufficient time not only to study the documents but also to prepare questions for the expert, which would mean that he would be testifying in court only once. What I have just said regarding the Defence will be a problem for the Prosecution during the Defence case when the Defence brings its own expert witnesses to testify in court. Therefore, our submission would be, and request, that you review this request in that light. And regarding 66 bis, I think that the spirit of the Rule really relates to the period prior to the beginning of trial in essence, though it can also be applied in the course of the trial itself. That would be my submission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, we have a question here which was not in our minds when we granted you a month-long delay. Do you intend to have the witness called back or not? The answer may be that that depends on your re-reading and studying of the document, but I would like to have an idea. Do you imagine calling the witness back to cross-examine him or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're asking me about this particular witness, most probably no. I can't say with certainty, but most probably no. But in principle, if such a situation were to occur again, the answer would probably be yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that Mr. Petrusic was not going to call back the witness, and that is why we gave you this time to review the document. Have you anything to add or shall I convey my ruling?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, nothing more, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end of the day, as Mr. Visnjic has said, the Chamber has been asked for some guidelines, some guidance. So we don't really have a particular issue to rule on, but we will convey to you what we think about the matter, what we think about the matter right now, regarding this particular issue. I think that it is clear, Professor Brunborg, in answer to a question by Mr. Petrusic, said that this booklet or this document was an annex to his report and, therefore, I think that we cannot go so far as to ask the Prosecutor to send to the Defence all the materials which the expert witness used to compile his report. Perhaps the whole Demography Institute of Norway would have to come here to the courtroom. Of course, I'm exaggerating, but it is also true that we cannot limit ourselves to the eight- or nine-page report of the expert witness. Therefore, in this particular case, I think that it was reasonable for the report of the expert witness to have been accompanied with this document, which was very closely and directly used as a basis for the whole study. We agree with the interpretation Mr. Harmon made of the Rules, but I think that in this particular case it is quite possible that when the Prosecutor intends to use this document as an exhibit to be tendered, it is quite reasonable. And, anyway, there is no problem in sending it to the Defence, I think. So as I said, Mr. Visnjic asked for the opinion of the Chamber. This is our opinion. But I think that we will have to reconsider this question again at a status conference, and then we can go into the practical matters, because Mr. Visnjic has already gone further by saying that, "We would like to know, for our own guidance, what we should provide to the Prosecution when our turn comes." So I think that for the moment, the question is closed regarding this particular case, but I think we shall have to reopen the discussion at a status conference so as to be able to organise our work properly. I think now we have to switch over to hearing time, which means resume our proceedings. I think Mr. Harmon was talking about a 20 or something -- 29-minute video, exactly the amount of time we need before a break. Mr. Harmon, is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we can now have the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before we play Prosecutor's Exhibit 56, which is the number on the video, I would ask that the documents that accompany that video, which are 56A, the English transcript, and 56B, the French transcript, be distributed. And to put this video into context, into proper context, let me explain what Your Honours will see and what the audience will see. This exhibit, for the record, is an exhibit, as I said, that was taken from a Rule 61 hearing conducted in 1996. For purposes of the record, the Defence has consented to this video being played, and therefore we did not call Mr. Mesic, who is the person testifying, to the stand live. In 1996, we had available -- the Office of the Prosecutor had available to us film footage taken in Potocari in July -- on July the 12th and the 13th. I've introduced into evidence those clips of the film showing men being separated from women. When we received that film, we asked representatives of the Bosnian government to attempt to identify the individuals who were in the film, the Muslim men who were being separated and the Muslim men who were being detained at a location called the "white house". Prior to the testimony of Mr. Mesic in 1996, I was informed that a certain number of those people had been identified, and therefore Mr. Mesic came to the Rule 61 hearing, he was shown the film, and he made those identifications. Now, with that in mind, I need to also inform the Chamber that on the 10th of February of this year, I was informed that one of the individuals who had been identified by Mr. Mesic had been incorrectly identified, and that identification relates to an individual who will be seen in the Photograph Z37, an individual by the name of Mustafa Mujcinovic. It turned out the individual who had identified Mr. Mujcinovic was mistaken, and subsequently the Bosnian government learned of that mistaken identification. Mr. Mesic, when he testified, believed that to be an accurate identification, but with that correction by the Bosnian government, then this film can be properly viewed. The reference to the Z37 will be found in the transcripts that I've provided to Your Honours. One last piece of information for Your Honours. I have been informed that the film, which is the official record of the Rule 61 hearing and which was provided to us for purposes of this exhibit, lacks a matter of minutes at the end of the film. A few minutes are missing. However, I'm also informed that the French and the English transcripts of that proceeding are complete. So with that introduction, Mr. President and Your Honours, if we could now proceed by dimming the lights and we could see Mr. Mesic's testimony in Prosecutor's Exhibit 56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, perhaps before we start viewing the video and for the record, I should like to ask the Defence if what Mr. Harmon is saying is true and are you accepting the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we are, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This was only for the purposes of the record. Thank you very much. Now we can begin with the viewing. [Videotape played]. ANSWER: [Voiceover] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. ANSWER: [Voiceover] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You have been called as a witness by the Prosecution, so I'm going to ask Mr. Ostberg to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. QUESTION: Will you please state your name and also spell it for the record? ANSWER: [Voiceover] Pasaga Mesic. P-a-s-a-g-a, M-e-s-i-c. QUESTION: Would you also state your present occupation? ANSWER: [Voiceover] Head of the police department in Tuzla which, among other things, collects facts about crimes committed in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. QUESTION: Could you tell us about what this police department in Tuzla encompassed, the cities or places we have been talking about in the context of Srebrenica? ANSWER: [Voiceover] My department covered the territory of North-East Bosnia. Before the war, there was the administrative region of Tuzla. It belonged to the Tuzla region which, among other common municipalities, covers the municipalities of Srebrenica, Bratunac, and others. QUESTION: Thank you. Did you, in your office, try to identify missing people? ANSWER: [Voiceover] Yes, we did. QUESTION: How did you go about that? ANSWER: [Voiceover] We did it in several ways. The chief method was that when people expelled from Srebrenica arrived when the Serb army took the enclave of Srebrenica, in those places where the expelled were accommodated in their settlements, we conducted a questionnaire of all citizens of age who had arrived there. The questionnaire included -- in addition to the name and particulars, it also included a question of where their next of kin were. In those questionnaires, they listed the names of their close relatives who either had been kept by the Serb army in Potocari or tried to reach the free territory through the woods. Another question in the questionnaire was whether they had witnessed a murder or some other crime, that is, some other violation of international humanitarian law. QUESTION: Thank you. Can you provide the Court with the figure of numbers of missing people from the U.N. safe area of Srebrenica? ANSWER: [Voiceover] After we had collected all the information and facts in this and other ways, we were able to make some estimates about the number of persons missing. It is, however, still impossible to identify all the missing persons. The information we have gathered so far says that during the attack of the Serb army against the enclave, that is, the protected zone of Srebrenica, between 6.000 to 6.500 people went missing. QUESTION: And what means did you use to reach this result, apart from what you already told us about this questionnaire? ANSWER: [Voiceover] In addition to this, we also used lists of missing persons compiled by the International Committee of the Red Cross, and that is their office in Tuzla, which was also supplied to the Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners in Tuzla. We also used information from the lists of missing persons compiled by representatives of the municipalities of Srebrenica, Bratunac and Vlasenica, and on the basis of all this information and by subtracting from that number the of persons who arrived in the free territory in the meantime, including the surrender of persons to IFOR in Zvornik, it was 3.469 [sic] missing persons. QUESTION: Will you name the figure again? I did not quite get it. ANSWER: [Voiceover] 9.349 persons. QUESTION: Thank you. Now, during this period, the free territory was reached by a certain number of members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina who managed to break through the Serb blockade. We do not have the exact figure because it is a military secret and therefore may not be divulged. However, on the basis of the information we have, we estimate it is about 30 per cent of the last figure I mentioned, which means that between 3.000 and 3.500 members of the army arrived in the free territory. And when this is subtracted from those 9.349, we arrive at the first figure, that is, that about 6.000 to 6.500 people are still missing. QUESTION: Thank you very much. Now I would like to turn to another matter, namely, photographs which I'm soon going to show you. I will first ask you this: Did the Office of the Prosecutor present you with photographs of prisoners from the Srebrenica enclave? ANSWER: [Voiceover] Yes. QUESTION: Do you know where these photographs came from? ANSWER: [Voiceover] No, I don't know that, but I know that the photographs were taken of a film which was in the possession of an investigating team of the Tribunal. QUESTION: What were you asked to do with these photos? ANSWER: [Voiceover] The investigator's team of the Tribunal asked us to try to identify those persons with those who had arrived in the territory, as they were showing men who were members of the Serb army in Potocari and other places in the Srebrenica area were separated by the Serb army from their families and then taken into an unknown direction. QUESTION: What methods did you use to try to identify these prisoners? ANSWER: [Voiceover] We began by showing those photographs to the expelled people from Srebrenica in refugee camps in which they were accommodated. But since they were scattered all over the territory, almost throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we were not able to identify them for those missing persons. A fortnight ago, we used the cantonal television of Tuzla and we broadcasted those photographs and invited anyone who could identify anyone in those photographs to come to our office and then identify any of those persons who they could recognise or they knew from the photographs that we had. QUESTION: Thank you. How many photographs were you presented with? ANSWER: [Voiceover] We were shown 30 photographs. QUESTION: And were you able to determine the identities of the persons in these photos? ANSWER: [Voiceover] Yes. We identified 28 persons. QUESTION: Thank you. Now I'm going to show you some photos, and you tell us what you found out concerning the people we are going to show you. I think it is, in total, 16 photos, and the first one is Exhibit 8A. Can the Court see that photograph also? I now ask you, can you identify any persons on that photo? Were you able to identify any one of them? ANSWER: [Voiceover] On this photograph, we identified three persons. QUESTION: Thank you. Please proceed. Again, my question was: Can you identify any one of these people on that photograph? ANSWER: [Voiceover] Yes. The person I'm pointing at now is Sevko Mujic, son of Omer. QUESTION: Do you have a pointer? Can we point with -- has he something to point with? On the ELMO, I think you have to do it. ANSWER: [Voiceover] The person I'm pointing at now is Sevko Mujic. QUESTION: Who did identify him? ANSWER: [Voiceover] He was identified by a neighbour. QUESTION: Can you tell us about his fate? ANSWER: [Voiceover] He disappeared, he's missing, and nothing is known about his fate. QUESTION: Thank you. Are there any other persons on this photo that you can identify? ANSWER: [Voiceover] Yes. QUESTION: And who is this person? ANSWER: [Voiceover] This is Ahmo Mehmedovic, son of Sulejman, age 58. He was identified by a neighbour. QUESTION: And his fate? ANSWER: [Voiceover] He's also missing. QUESTION: Thank you. Any other on this photo? ANSWER: [Voiceover] Yes. This person here, this is Meho Mehmedovic, also son of Sulejman, Ahmo's brother, age 56, also identified by neighbours. QUESTION: And his fate? ANSWER: [Voiceover] He's missing too. QUESTION: Thank you. As Your Honours may recall, these are photos that were shown by our investigator Rene Ruez during his examination. So you have seen them before, and now we show them again just for this purpose. Can I have Exhibit 8B, please. Can you identify anybody on this photograph? ANSWER: [Voiceover] It is this person. He was also in Exhibit 8A. This is Meho Mehmedovic. QUESTION: And who identified him? ANSWER: [Voiceover] He was identified by his neighbour or, rather, two persons who were his neighbours while they were in the area of Srebrenica. QUESTION: What do we know about him? ANSWER: [Voiceover] He's missing. QUESTION: Now we look at Exhibit 10B. Can you identify anybody on this photo? ANSWER: [Voiceover] Yes. QUESTION: And that is? ANSWER: [Voiceover] This person's name is Kasim Hafizovic, son of Mehmed, age 58, and was identified by his close relatives. QUESTION: And what do we know about him? ANSWER: [Voiceover] He's missing too. QUESTION: Is there anybody else on this photo who you can -- ANSWER: [Voiceover] Yes. Senahid Hafizovic, son of Mehmed, aged 54, also identified by neighbours, also on the list of missing persons. QUESTION: Thank you. We go on to Exhibit 11A, and we can really see two persons on it. Can you identify them? ANSWER: [Voiceover] Yes, this person is Misa Efendic, son of Meho, age 63, identified by a neighbour, also on the list of missing persons. QUESTION: Thank you. And the other one? ANSWER: [Voiceover] The other person is Ibro Huseinovic, son of Ahmo, aged 51, identified by his close relatives, listed as a missing person. QUESTION: Can we now please go to Exhibit 12D. Do you have any -- can we -- I can't see anything on my screen for the moment. Here we are. Thank you. ANSWER: [Voiceover] Only this person was identified on this photograph. This is Nazif Krdzic, aged 54, identified by his colleague. QUESTION: And his fate? ANSWER: [Voiceover] He's also missing. QUESTION: And now, please, we go to Exhibit 13A. Could you point us out the people there? Yes, and who is that? ANSWER: [Voiceover] Yes. This is Bajro Malkic, son of Hilmo, aged 53, identified by his relatives, listed as a missing person. QUESTION: Thank you. Any other people on this photo? ANSWER: [Voiceover] Next person is Mevludin Pasagic, aged 56, identified by his close relatives on the list of missing persons. One more person on this photograph, Hamza Gudic, aged 52, identified by colleagues. He's also on the list of missing persons. QUESTION: Thank you. And then I will ask for number 13B. ANSWER: [Voiceover] Here we see Hamza Gudic again. We saw him in number 13A. Then this person here, his name is Idriz Suljic, son of Sanaban, aged 60, identified by friends, on the list of missing persons. QUESTION: Yes. ANSWER: [Voiceover] This person here is Ibrahim Jelkic, son of Bahrija, aged 59, identified by a friend, also on the list of missing persons. QUESTION: Thank you. Can I ask for Exhibit number 14B. You will recognise him. That was the person who was forced to call out for his comrades in the hills. Yes, please? ANSWER: [Voiceover] This person here is Ramo Osmanovic, son of Omer, age 42, identified by relatives, on the list of missing persons. On this photograph, we also identified this person here. There is Miralem Mujic, son of Rasim, aged 47, identified by close relatives, also on the list of missing persons. QUESTION: Thank you. May I have Exhibit number 15B? You do also, Your Honours, recognise him. That was the person who was interviewed by a television reporter. Yes, please? ANSWER: [Voiceover] This person is Ramo Mustafic, son of Meho, age 54, identified by relatives. QUESTION: Thank you. Now I would ask for Exhibit number 16A. ANSWER: [Voiceover] On this photograph we see Salih Salihovic, aged 49, identified by friends, on the list of missing persons. QUESTION: Thank you. May I ask for number 17B. ANSWER: [Voiceover] On this photograph we identified two persons. This is Ramo Kabilovic, son of Hajro, aged 34, was identified by close relatives, on the list of missing persons. In the middle and behind him on the stretcher is Mujo Mesanovic, son of Abdulah, aged 22, identified by close relatives, on the list of missing persons. QUESTION: Thank you. I would ask for Exhibit number 18A. ANSWER: [Voiceover] This person here is Salih Isbisevic, son of Ibrahim, 36 years old. He was identified by his close relatives, and he's on the list of missing persons. QUESTION: Thank you and now 19B, please. ANSWER: [Voiceover] On this photograph, this young man has been identified. His name is Almir Salcinovic, son of Turabija, 21 years old, and he was identified by a friend. Then Halil Gabeljic, son of Mahmut, who was identified by a friend and who is also on the list of missing persons. QUESTION: Both of these people are missing, correct. ANSWER: [Voiceover] Yes. QUESTION: Thank you. That takes us to 20B, please. ANSWER: [Voiceover] This person's name is Muhamed Malagic, son of Ramiz, 23 years old. He was identified by his close relatives and he is on the list of missing persons now. QUESTION: Thank you. And now 21B, please. ANSWER: [Voiceover] On this photograph, Nezir Ibisevic was identified. He's the son of Juso, 20 years old. He was identified by his friends. He's on the missing-persons' list now. QUESTION: Now we're going to show you the last photograph, and that is 22B. ANSWER: [Voiceover] This person's name is Bajazit Delic, son of Amil. He was identified by distant relatives, and he's on the missing-persons' list now. This here is Mustafa Mujcinovic, son of Mujo, 38 years old, was identified by an acquaintance, and he's on the missing-persons' list now. QUESTION: All these people we have now shown photos of, are they all missing? ANSWER: [Voiceover] Yes, all these persons are on the missing-persons' list. We said that 28 persons have been identified. We saw 26 persons, because two persons reached the free territory and their photographs, for security reasons, we will not be showing. One man is 62 years old, and a boy who's only 14. QUESTION: Thank you. And all the others are missing. ANSWER: [Voiceover] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTRBERG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This concludes the questions I have to put to you, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Do you have a question, Madam Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Mr. Pasaga Mesic, you spoke of about 6.000, 6.500 missing persons. Could you tell the Court how many are men, how many are women, how many are children? ANSWER: [Voiceover] No. At this moment I cannot tell the Court that because we do not know exactly even the number of missing people nor the composition of those missing persons. Since the activities to complete data on missing persons are still underway and, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is formed a commission for missing persons which should also take part take in the final establishment of the number of missing persons and their composition during the takeover by the Srebrenica enclave by the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: So that means that you couldn't say if mostly they are elderly people. ANSWER: [Voiceover] Mostly they were males over 17 years of age, since most of the women and children were transported out of Srebrenica ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That concludes the tape, Mr. President. As I said, part of it is missing but the transcripts are complete, and we would tender as exhibits copies of Prosecutor's Exhibit 56, which is the tape; and 56A, the English transcript of the proceedings; and 56B, the French transcript of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, do we know whether any of those people who are identified in the video and were then on the missing list have since been found?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that. All I know is that the Bosnia government has informed me that one person was misidentified. Whether that person was misidentified and is now alive, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, do you have any objections in respect of this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The exhibits will be admitted into evidence. I think that this is a very convenient time for a break. However, before the break, I think I should mention something for the benefit of the public. Mr. Harmon, you stated that we should go into closed session to discuss the work of the next week. Can we do it before the break or maybe after the break, or maybe we can discuss it now and then after the break inform the public about the schedule for next week. So we will now go into closed session. After the closed session, there will be a break, and we will be back around half past 1.00. Closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Manning, thank you very much for coming back. We're going to treat this as the continuation of your testimony, and you are now going to answer questions which I think Mr. Visnjic is going to put to you within the framework of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. As we said when asking for the delay for Mr. Manning, most of the questions that we had prepared for him have been answered for us by the expert witnesses, so that our cross-examination of Mr. Manning will be very brief and consists of only a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Manning. Your report of the 16th of May contains parts which are written in italics. I hope the interpreters will be able to interpret this.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you explain? Are those parts, also a component part of expert findings or are they another kind of proof?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you would have to refer to a specific section of italics. I believe each separate grave area has an italic area, if that's what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On page 5 of your report, and items 1, 2, 3, and then again on page 6. In fact, on every page containing descriptions of grave sites, there is what one might call an introductory paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's the section that I've marked with italics, if you like. It was simply to highlight the introduction, if you like, to each of the crime scenes in that I was trying to summarise it. That was just to highlight the introduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Were those parts taken from expert reports or were they compiled in the form of an introduction to the report?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the main, they were taken either from the indictment or from a summary of the witness such as you see with Witness S40 on the bottom of page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question relates to page 20 of your report, and page 21, containing tables on ligatures and blindfolds. I have noted a certain discrepancy in the numbers given in this report and the numbers that were given to us by the experts. So I should like to ask you about one or two specific examples to see whether you can explain the difference for me. On page 20, it is stated that the total number of ligatures for Kozluk is 168. At the same time, I compared that number with the number given by Dr. Clark in his report, on page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I have that page of the report, and I would like to ask the usher for his assistance, to show it to Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I think that the number of ligatures in your report is slightly higher than the one given in his.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just looking at those figures, my indication of the number of ligatures is higher. I believe I spoke about that during my evidence in chief, in that I looked at what was found at the site, what was found by the pathologists, and what was found loose, if you like, at the morgue, and I indicated then, I believe, that there would be differences in what the archaeologists found and what the pathologists in the morgue found and what I said was the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The number that you gave, would that be a compilation of all the numbers found by the anthropologists and the pathologists or is there another source that collected evidence?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: My figure represents ligatures in this case that were located during the exhumation and autopsy process only; that is, ligatures found at the grave site, ligatures found at the morgue site by those people you mentioned, plus also scientific officers examining the artefacts at the morgue. I assume that Dr. Clark did not examine all the ligatures, specifically ones that weren't located with the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that same page, it is stated that at the Petkovci dam, one ligature was found. However, the Prosecution has shown us two exhibits showing two ligatures. One is Exhibit number 22/8, and the other one is 131/1. This is Exhibit 22/8, showing a ligature found by Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez during his stay there in April 1997. I think that is the final date established. And Exhibit 131/1, showing another ligature, was produced during your testimony in chief. My question is whether you could explain to us this particular discrepancy. A second part of that question is the actual technique applied to collect this kind of physical evidence or artefacts.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer the first part of your question, this ligature here, the string ligature marked DG-118, was located during the autopsy -- sorry, exhumation process at the dam conducted by Professor Wright. I included that as a ligature located at Petkovci dam or the dam near Petkovci on the basis that it was found during that process, and I was summarising evidence located during the exhumation/autopsy process. The other ligature which is shown in this photograph was, as you pointed out, located by Mr. Ruez, not as part of the exhumation/autopsy process. It wasn't examined by the archaeologists or the scientific officers or by the pathologists. Therefore, as I said, it was a conservative number of ligatures and blindfolds, and that one was not counted by myself as part of this process.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain in a little greater detail the technique, the method applied regarding, for example, Exhibit 22/8. It was found on site and then what?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to this exhibit here?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: For example, that one, yes.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not present when that item was located. Indeed, I wasn't at the Tribunal. Mr. Ruez handled this exhibit, so I'm afraid you'll have to ask him those details.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But generally speaking, for instance, Exhibit 131, I'm interested in the actual procedure of registering and safekeeping of these artefacts.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to this item, DG-118, and I have to generalise because I haven't got the details of this particular item in front of me, but when an exhumation is conducted, each item or body that is identified, the individual who finds it or identifies it calls out to the register keeper or a scientific officer present at the site for a number. The process has changed and evolved from 1998, but it's essentially the same. A number was issued for that item. It was either tagged immediately or tagged, and by "tagged" I mean that little metal tag that you see in that photograph or some other tag, removed from the grave, placed in a bag, reported on a ledger which would then accompany that item to the morgue. It may be that that item stayed with the body and is placed in the body bag, and it would then be removed at the morgue on examination. Again speaking generally, it could be that that item would not be discovered until it came to the morgue. It may be dirty or tangled with other things, in which case it would be cleaned, registered at the morgue, photographed, bagged, and placed into an exhibit locker or room. Basically, that's the general processing of an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Manning, according to the evidence produced by the Prosecution so far, and judging by the statement of witnesses who, in part of their testimony, claimed that in the area from Nova Kasaba to Konjevic Polje, while a column of males was going through the woods in the direction of Zvornik, that in that area there were numerous ambushes and a certain number of casualties. In the course of your investigations, were you aware of the fact of the burial place of those victims who fell as casualties during these events?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of the burial of those individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: According to the evidence produced by the Prosecution also, and judging by the statements of witnesses, one can infer that in the area of Bajkovici, of Zvornik, there were also armed conflicts between a column that was breaking through to the territory of the Federation. I have reviewed very briefly the list of missing persons, and, for instance, under the letter "A" alone, that is, persons whose surnames begin with the letter "A", the place of disappearance for 50 persons under that letter of the alphabet, Bajkovici and Udrc, territory in Zvornik municipality, are given. Also, according to certain sources, the Serb forces alone in a single day had more than 100 men put out of action; some killed, some wounded. Do you perhaps know where and whether the victims of those conflicts were buried?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Mr. President, that ends my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Harmon, have you any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Fouad Riad, do you have any questions? Madam Judge Wald, have you any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: During your testimony, Mr. Manning, I don't have the chart in front of me but I believe there was a chart that showed the graves that had been disturbed, the primary graves that had been disturbed, and those that had not, and the secondary graves. My question is basically whether or not, based upon your observation and research, you were able to come up with any hypothesis or clues as to why particular primary graves were disturbed, relocated to secondary graves, and others were left alone, based upon their location or any other factor that you might may have come across?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could surmise that graves that were undisturbed seemed to be in a particular area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Which area?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The graves around Cerska, Konjevic Polje, Nova Kasaba. I assume that because of that location, it was a difficulty in disturbing them or some other reason that they were not disturbed. I also believe that at least for the case of some of the graves, they were easily identified, particularly in light of the aerial images that were released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So just to nail that down, the first group that you said there would be difficulty in disturbing them, those were less accessible?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, no less accessible than Cancari road or -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, they were less accessible than some of the other primary graves that were disturbed or not?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that's the reason. As I say, I believe it may be due to the location. Those graves are as accessible as the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But when you say "location", why?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to answer that simply by saying that they seemed to be graves that are grouped together that have not been disturbed. So for some reason that I don't know, those graves were not disturbed. Perhaps they were too close to something, perhaps they had been in a different -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay, all right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. So, Mr. Manning, I think that we have finished your testimony. I think there are no exhibits to deal with in this case. Is that correct, Mr. Harmon, Mr. Visnjic? I don't think we have any outstanding exhibits to tender, or reports. The report is Exhibit 150, I think, is it not? No, 140. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In the course of Mr. Manning's direct examination, the exhibits were tendered and accepted by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Everything has been dealt with. Thank you very much, Mr. Manning, for coming to the courtroom and for answering the questions put to you. We are now going to adjourn. For the benefit of the public, I have to say that the whole day tomorrow, hearings will be held in closed session. So from the standpoint of the public, the case is closed for this week. So we will be resuming this trial, but in a different framework. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: 2.13 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 2nd day of June, 2000, at 9.30 a.m.
